newsitem.title: USA: Clinton reviewing late term abortion compromise.
newsitem.headline: Clinton reviewing late term abortion compromise.

text.p: The White House said on Tuesday it was "possible" President Clinton, who has vowed to veto a ban on so-called partial birth abortions, could support a proposed compromise to restrict such late-term procedures.

The Senate this week is likely to vote on a Republican proposal to ban partial birth abortions except to save the life of the woman. But chief sponsor Rick Santorum, a Pennsylvania Republican, acknowledged that he is about five votes shy of a veto-proof 67 votes.
Clinton vetoed that measure last year and has vowed to do so again.

Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota told reporters that his alternative proposal appeared to be gaining "a good deal of interest and support" but Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said he doubts Daschle will round up the votes. "The Daschle alternative probably will not pass," said Lott, a Mississippi Republican.

"I think that we are looking very carefully at Sen. Daschle's proposed language and we believe that it's possible for the White House to support that language," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said. He stressed, however, that the White House was "completing a review" of the bill and that a recommendation had not been presented to Clinton.

The procedure, which opponents call partial birth abortion and which can also be referred to as dilation and extraction, involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and removal of the foetus.

Recognising public discomfort with this procedure and other late-term abortion methods but believing that the Republican version inadequately protects a woman's health, Daschle drafted an alternative that would ban all abortions after a foetus is viable, or capable of surviving outside the womb.
Daschle's plan makes exceptions if a woman's life is in danger or if she faces "grievous" physical health problems late in her pregnancy.

It would apply to all surgical techniques used in late pregnancy, including partial birth, but would not ban that controversial procedure earlier in pregnancy. Many of these procedures are believed to take place in the second trimester.

The Republican-backed partial birth abortion ban, which could face a vote as soon as Thursday, would outlaw all partial birth procedures, at any point in the pregnancy. It would make exceptions to save a woman's life but has no provisions for health, including preventing damage to her reproductive organs.
Santorum, the Senate sponsor, derided Daschle's alternative as one big loophole that would not stop partial birth procedures, which he calls a "barbaric procedure" and has likened to "infanticide."
"It's a farce," he said of the Daschle proposal.
Debate had been expected to start on the Senate floor late Tuesday but was delayed at least a day by the scramble for votes and unrelated Senate business.
Forty-one states already have some restrictions on late term abortions. Daschle said his legislation would not override them and would apply only to the remaining nine states.
The Supreme Court's 1973 Roe versus Wade ruling granting women a right to abortion does allow states to regulate abortions in the final trimester of pregnancy.
Clinton's expected support for the Daschle measure drew fire from leaders of the Southern Baptist Convention.

"We write to beg you to reconsider your continued defence of the killing of living premature babies by the brutal partial birth method," the leaders said in a letter to Clinton, himself a Southern Baptist.

Opponents of the ban have said it hampers women's constitutional right to choose abortion, but even some abortion rights supporters have been swayed by a graphic campaign for the ban. Ads include line drawings of foetus's neck being pierced by scissors.
The House voted 295-136 on March 20 to pass the ban.

Television advertisements sponsored by the anti-abortion Child Protection Fund were being aimed at seven states where senators were believed to be wavering: Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Louisiana, Nebraska and Wisconsin.
